long.description:
The Black Death killed half of Europe in six years — and it arrived on twelve ships. How the plague of 1347-1353 remade the world forever.

In the winter of 1349, villages stood empty, wheat rotted in the fields, and church bells rang for no one. This is the story of how a bacterium hiding in the fur of rats rode the Silk Road to a besieged port called Caffa, sailed to Sicily aboard twelve Genoese galleys, and then rewrote everything: wages, faith, medicine, and the place of women in the world. What strikes me most about this story is not the death — it is how quickly the world rebuilt itself, and how much of our modern life was born in those terrible years. Imagine being there: a street you have known all your life, suddenly silent — and then, slowly, alive again. Years ago, I stood above an old plague pit in London, where thousands sleep beneath a quiet parking lot, and I have never forgotten it. In my view, the Black Death was history's cruelest teacher.
